newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN MP'S BID TO BREAK DEADLOCK ON DI RUPO.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN MP'S BID TO BREAK DEADLOCK ON DI RUPO.

text.p: Belgian politicians tried on Wednesday to break the deadlock on how to deal with allegations of under-age sex against Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, with signs of strain evident inside the governing coalition.

Di Rupo, a Francophone Socialist, has already been cleared of allegations in one case file that he had sex with boys under the legal age of consent of 16 years, and he denies the mostly anonymous charges in a second file.
His own party and its sister Flemish Socialists say there is no case to answer. The opposition French- and Dutch speaking Liberals are calling for his head.
In the middle stand the Francophone and Flemish Christian Democratic Parties which together with the Socialists make up the country's centre-left coalition.

On Wednesday parliamentary members of the Socialist parties boycotted a speech to the house on justice reforms by Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, a Christian Democrat, in protest at the lack of support Di Rupo was getting.
It is the third consecutive day that the special commission has tried to decide on the fate of the number two in the Belgian government.
It is faced essentially with three possibilities. It can throw out the allegations, ask for further investigations or indict Di Rupo which would automatically force him to resign.
Any decision must be endorsed by the full parliament.

The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court and the only one capable of judging a minister, has proposed another option, bypassing the cumbersome parliamentary procedure and allowing it to in effect receive any allegations against a minister.

However, in the climate of suspicion in Belgium between the judiciary and politicians, and with the deep public distrust of the system, this would be the equivalent of parliamentarians declaring open season on themselves.

The Di Rupo affair has been another nail in the coffin of Belgian public confidence, shaken since the arrest in August of child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four more.

In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in support of the victims and their families in a demonstration that crossed the country's language divide and became a show of disgust as a system deemed to be corrupt.

There have also been floods of denunciations of all types and against all sorts of people, with child rights groups reporting hundreds of letters a day and a special police hot line having received thousands of calls.
In response the government has rushed through a series of legal reforms, and the leaders of the main political parties on Saturday began a process that should lead to long-awaited political changes.

But Belgian politics received another blow on Monday when Jean-Pierre Grafe, a minister in a French-speaking regional government who has also been accused of paedophilia, unexpectedly announced his resignation.
He said he was innocent but could not continue to function in the current over-heated climate.

The Cour de Cassation on Tuesday handed a report to the French-speaking government on the allegations against Grafe, and Belga news agency said chief public prosecutor Eliane Lieckendael had asked for him to be indicted.
